Differentially Private PC Scores

Source: vignettes/theory-dp-score.Rmd
theory-dp-score.Rmd

In ordinary PCA, a score plot displays the projected coordinates of individual observations along selected principal component (PC) directions. However, directly releasing these coordinates may reveal sensitive information about individual observations. To address this issue, the dppca package constructs a differentially private (DP) two-dimensional score histogram, which summarizes the distribution of projected scores without directly releasing individual coordinates.

The procedure involves three main steps: obtaining private PC directions, constructing a private plotting frame, and estimating a private score histogram. Also, synthetic points can then be generated from the private histogram as a post-processing step, without requiring additional privacy budget.

This article describes the mathematical construction and privacy accounting of these methods. For implementation details, plotting options, and examples, see the DP Score Plot Tutorial. For background, see PCA Background and Theory of DP Loading.

1. Two-dimensional PC scores

Let X=(x1,…,xn)⊤∈ℝn×pX=(x_1,\ldots,x_n)^\top\in\mathbb R^{n\times p} contain nn observations and pp numeric variables. Let Ṽ=(ṽ1,…,ṽp)\widetilde V=(\widetilde v_1,\ldots,\widetilde v_p) be an orthonormal matrix of privately estimated PC directions. For selected, distinct components a,b∈{1,…,p}a,b\in\{1,\ldots,p\}, define

Y=XṼ,s̃i=(xi⊤ṽaxi⊤ṽb)∈ℝ2,i=1,…,n. Y=X\widetilde V, \qquad \widetilde s_i=\begin{pmatrix} x_i^\top\widetilde v_a\\ x_i^\top\widetilde v_b \end{pmatrix}\in\mathbb R^2, \qquad i=1,\ldots,n.

The projected coordinates s̃i\widetilde s_i are needed internally to estimate the score distribution, but are not returned with a private-only result. Unlike an ordinary PCA score scatter plot, the released visualization is a private histogram of these two-dimensional points.

2. Private plotting frame

A histogram needs a rectangular plotting region, called its frame. Taking coordinate minima, maxima, or quantiles directly from private observations would leak data. Instead, the frame is constructed with the private quantile mechanisms of Durfee (2023).

Let εF\varepsilon_F be the epsilon budget allocated to frame estimation. The algorithm uses three pure-DP quantile releases, each with budget εF/3\varepsilon_F/3: two coordinate medians and one radial quantile.

2.1. Private coordinate medians

For the selected score coordinates, estimate a private center

c̃1=𝒬εF/3({si1}i=1n,0.5),c̃2=𝒬εF/3({si2}i=1n,0.5),c̃=(c̃1,c̃2)⊤. \widetilde c_1 =\mathcal Q_{\varepsilon_F/3}(\{s_{i1}\}_{i=1}^n,0.5), \qquad \widetilde c_2 =\mathcal Q_{\varepsilon_F/3}(\{s_{i2}\}_{i=1}^n,0.5), \qquad \widetilde c=(\widetilde c_1,\widetilde c_2)^\top.

Here 𝒬ε(⋅,q)\mathcal Q_{\varepsilon}(\cdot,q) denotes the fully unbounded private quantile mechanism at level qq.

2.2. Private radial quantile and square frame

Next, compute the distance of each score from the private center:

ri=∥s̃i−c̃∥2=(s̃i1−c̃1)2+(s̃i2−c̃2)2. r_i=\|\widetilde s_i-\widetilde c\|_2 =\sqrt{(\widetilde s_{i1}-\widetilde c_1)^2+(\widetilde s_{i2}-\widetilde c_2)^2}.

Since ri≥0r_i\ge0, the implementation applies the one-sided unbounded private quantile mechanism with public lower bound zero to estimate the 0.99 quantile:

R̃=𝒬εF/3upper({ri}i=1n,0.99). \widetilde R =\mathcal Q^{\mathrm{upper}}_{\varepsilon_F/3} (\{r_i\}_{i=1}^n,0.99).

The radius is enlarged by a fixed factor 1+α1+\alpha, with α=0.20\alpha=0.20 in the package. Writing RF=(1+α)R̃R_F=(1+\alpha)\widetilde R, the frame becomes

F=[c̃1−RF,c̃1+RF]×[c̃2−RF,c̃2+RF]. F=[\widetilde c_1-R_F,\widetilde c_1+R_F] \times[\widetilde c_2-R_F,\widetilde c_2+R_F].

Conditional on the required mechanism assumptions, sequential composition of the three pure-DP quantile releases gives the frame allocation (εF,0)(\varepsilon_F,0).

3. Histogram grid and sensitivity

Divide the private frame into mxm_x horizontal-axis bins and mym_y vertical-axis bins, giving J=mxmyJ=m_xm_y rectangular cells B1,…,BJB_1,\ldots,B_J. The numbers of bins are public tuning choices.

Let hF(s̃i)h_F(\widetilde s_i) be the grid cell assigned to score s̃i\widetilde s_i. If a coordinate falls outside the frame, the implementation assigns it to the corresponding boundary bin, rather than dropping that observation. For cell jj, define

cj=∑i=1n𝟏{hF(s̃i)=j},pj=cjn,j=1,…,J. c_j=\sum_{i=1}^n\mathbf1\{h_F(\widetilde s_i)=j\}, \qquad p_j=\frac{c_j}{n}, \qquad j=1,\ldots,J.

Since every score is assigned to a cell, ∑jcj=n\sum_j c_j=n and ∑jpj=1\sum_jp_j=1 before noise is introduced.

Under fixed-size replacement adjacency, replacing one observation can remove one count from a cell and add one count to another. Conditional on fixed private directions, a fixed frame, and appropriate preprocessing, the histogram count vector c=(c1,…,cJ)⊤c=(c_1,\ldots,c_J)^\top satisfies

Δ1(c)≤2,Δ2(c)≤2. \Delta_1(c)\le2, \qquad \Delta_2(c)\le\sqrt{2}.

4. Private histogram estimators

Two histogram methods are available: an additive Gaussian histogram and a stability-based sparse histogram. Both operate on the same privately estimated frame, but their perturbation and normalization rules differ. Write (εH,δH)(\varepsilon_H,\delta_H) for the histogram privacy allocation.

4.1. Additive Gaussian histogram

The additive method perturbs all JJ bin counts, including empty bins, using a Gaussian perturbation by Wasserman and Zhou, 2010:

c̃j=cj+Zj,Zj∼iidN(0,σH2),σH=22log(1.25/δH)εH. \widetilde c_j=c_j+Z_j, \qquad Z_j\overset{\mathrm{iid}}\sim N(0,\sigma_H^2), \qquad \sigma_H=\frac{\sqrt{2}\sqrt{2\log(1.25/\delta_H)}}{\varepsilon_H}.

The factor 2\sqrt{2} comes from the count vector’s ℓ2\ell_2-sensitivity. Negative noisy counts are replaced by zero and the remaining values are normalized:

p̃jadd=max{c̃j,0}∑h=1Jmax{c̃h,0}. \widetilde p_j^{\mathrm{add}} =\frac{\max\{\widetilde c_j,0\}} {\sum_{h=1}^J\max\{\widetilde c_h,0\}}.

The truncation and normalization are post-processing and do not themselves spend privacy budget. If all truncated noisy counts are zero, the dppca stops with an error instead of returning probabilities. For the related algorithm, see Additive DP histogram.

4.2. Stability-based sparse histogram

The sparse approach is designed for grids containing many empty cells. It perturbs only nonempty empirical bin proportions, following the stability-based histogram idea discussed by Karwa and Vadhan (2018).

For the nn observations, define the Laplace noise scale and threshold

bH=2nεH,TH=1n+2log(2/δH)nεH. b_H=\frac{2}{n\varepsilon_H}, \qquad T_H=\frac1n+\frac{2\log(2/\delta_H)}{n\varepsilon_H}.

For each cell with cj>0c_j>0, draw Lj∼Laplace(0,bH)L_j\sim\operatorname{Laplace}(0,b_H) and set

qj={max{pj+Lj,0},max{pj+Lj,0}≥TH,0,otherwise. q_j= \begin{cases} \max\{p_j+L_j,0\},&\max\{p_j+L_j,0\}\ge T_H,\\ 0,&\text{otherwise}. \end{cases}

For a cell with cj=0c_j=0, set qj=0q_j=0 without drawing noise. The result is

p̃jsparse={qj∑h=1Jqh,∑h=1Jqh>0,0,∑h=1Jqh=0. \widetilde p_j^{\mathrm{sparse}}= \begin{cases} \displaystyle\frac{q_j}{\sum_{h=1}^Jq_h},&\sum_{h=1}^Jq_h>0,\\[6pt] 0,&\sum_{h=1}^Jq_h=0. \end{cases}

Unlike the additive method, the sparse estimator can return an all-zero histogram when no cell passes the threshold. For the related algorithm, see the Sparse DP histogram.

5. Privacy budget allocation

A standalone score analysis has a loading budget for private directions and a score budget for the frame and histogram. Write

(εL,δL),(εscore,δscore). (\varepsilon_L,\delta_L),\qquad (\varepsilon_{\mathrm{score}},\delta_{\mathrm{score}}).

The dp_score()` subdivides the score budget as

εF=0.35εscore,δF=0,εH=0.65εscore,δH=δscore. \begin{aligned} \varepsilon_F&=0.35\,\varepsilon_{\mathrm{score}}, &\delta_F&=0,\\ \varepsilon_H&=0.65\,\varepsilon_{\mathrm{score}}, &\delta_H&=\delta_{\mathrm{score}}. \end{aligned}

The private frame uses its epsilon equally for two coordinate medians and one radial quantile. The histogram receives the remaining epsilon and all of the score delta. With a single histogram method and private directions, the nominal composition budget is

(εL+εF+εH,δL+δH)=(εL+εscore,δL+δscore). (\varepsilon_L+\varepsilon_F+\varepsilon_H, \;\delta_L+\delta_H) =(\varepsilon_L+\varepsilon_{\mathrm{score}}, \;\delta_L+\delta_{\mathrm{score}}).

6. Synthetic score sampling

The released private histogram represents an estimated distribution of projected scores, rather than the original observations. Synthetic score points can be generated from this distribution using either center or uniform sampling.

Let B1,…,BJB_1,\ldots,B_J denote the histogram bins, with private probabilities p̃1,…,p̃J\widetilde p_1,\ldots,\widetilde p_J. For each synthetic point, a bin index is first sampled according to

A∼Categorical(p̃1,…,p̃J). A\sim\operatorname{Categorical} (\widetilde p_1,\ldots,\widetilde p_J).

The coordinates are then generated using one of two methods.

  • Center sampling: Let cAc_A denote the center of the selected bin BAB_A. A synthetic point is generated by adding Gaussian noise to this center: S*=cA+Z. S^*=c_A+Z.

  • Uniform sampling: First, a point is drawn uniformly within the selected bin BAB_A, and Gaussian noise is then added: U∣A∼Uniform(BA),S*=U+Z. U\mid A\sim\operatorname{Uniform}(B_A), \qquad S^*=U+Z.

In both methods, the Gaussian noise is independently generated as

Z∼N2(0,γ2(Δx200Δy2)), Z\sim N_2\left( 0,\, \gamma^2 \begin{pmatrix} \Delta_x^2 & 0\\ 0 & \Delta_y^2 \end{pmatrix} \right),

where Δx\Delta_x and Δy\Delta_y are the histogram bin widths and γ\gamma is the smoothing multiplier specified by bandwidth_scale. The default values are γ=0.5\gamma=0.5 for center sampling and γ=0.25\gamma=0.25 for uniform sampling. Setting γ=0\gamma=0 removes the Gaussian noise.

7. Group-wise private score histograms

Suppose every observation has a group label gi∈𝒢g_i\in\mathcal G. With public, fixed group memberships, the procedure estimates one set of private directions and one private frame using all observations, then releases one histogram for each group on the same grid. Write

cj(g)=∑i=1n𝟏{gi=g,hF(s̃i)=j},g∈𝒢,j=1,…,J. c_j^{(g)} =\sum_{i=1}^n\mathbf1\{g_i=g,\ h_F(\widetilde s_i)=j\}, \qquad g\in\mathcal G,\ j=1,\ldots,J.

Each group applies the selected private histogram mechanism to its own counts and normalizes within that group.
When the groups form disjoint, publicly fixed subsets, parallel composition across groups can justify using the same histogram privacy allocation for every group of a single method. The shared direction and frame costs are paid once.

For related procedures, see Group-wise additive histogram and Group-wise sparse histogram.

8.1. Display centering

In ordinary PCA, the input data are typically mean-centered before projection, so the resulting PC scores have sample mean zero. In contrast, the dppca package does not automatically mean-center the input data, and the private projected scores are not necessarily centered at the origin.

To facilitate visual interpretation, the package provides an optional display-centering adjustment using the privately estimated frame center c̃=(c̃1,c̃2)⊤\widetilde c=(\widetilde c_1,\widetilde c_2)^\top defined in Section 2.1.

For each displayed coordinate ℓ∈{1,2}\ell\in\{1,2\}, define the display-centering adjustment as

cℓdisp={c̃ℓ,if center = TRUE,0,if center = FALSE. c_\ell^{\mathrm{disp}} = \begin{cases} \widetilde c_\ell, & \text{if center = TRUE},\\ 0, & \text{if center = FALSE}. \end{cases}

Let cdisp=(c1disp,c2disp)⊤c^{\mathrm{disp}}=(c_1^{\mathrm{disp}},c_2^{\mathrm{disp}})^\top. Each histogram cell BjB_j and synthetic score point S*S^* are displayed using the translated coordinates

Bjdisp=Bj−cdisp,S*,disp=S*−cdisp. B_j^{\mathrm{disp}}=B_j-c^{\mathrm{disp}}, \qquad S^{*,\mathrm{disp}}=S^*-c^{\mathrm{disp}}.

With center = TRUE (the default), the displayed frame becomes Fdisp=F−c̃F^{\mathrm{disp}}=F-\widetilde c, whose center is (0,0)(0,0). With center = FALSE, the original private frame coordinates are displayed without any shift.

For group-wise histograms, the same display-centering adjustment is applied to all groups. The ordinary PCA reference, when requested, already uses sample-mean-centered scores and a zero-centered reference frame.

Display centering is purely post-processing: it changes only the plotted coordinates without modifying the stored private estimates, histogram probabilities, or sampled points, and requires no additional privacy budget. The same adjustment is also used in the DP biplot to allow variable arrows to originate at (0,0)(0,0) in Section 3.2: DP biplot. In plot.dp_pca(), the center option is shared by the score and biplot displays.

For implementation details, plotting options, and examples, see the DP Score Plot Tutorial.

Karwa, V., and Vadhan, S. (2018). Finite sample differentially private confidence intervals. Proceedings of ITCS 2018, LIPIcs 94, 44:1–44:9. https://doi.org/10.4230/LIPIcs.ITCS.2018.44
